sysd-blocks-069.title: Content delivery networks: serving users from nearby
sysd-blocks-069.text:
A visitor in the UK opens a site hosted in the USA, and the page arrives from London. That is a content delivery network at work. A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them. Users fetch content from a nearby CDN node instead of the origin, the server where the content actually lives. The origin's servers then do not have to handle the requests the CDN fulfills. A close edge location is also much quicker than a full request to the origin.

CDNs arose in the late 1990s to relieve bottlenecks in the Internet's performance. They now serve a large portion of Internet content: web text, graphics and scripts, downloadable files, applications, live and on-demand streams, and social media services. Static files such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript, photos and videos are generally what a CDN serves, though it can deliver dynamic content too.

The benefits are reduced bandwidth costs, faster page loads, higher global availability and better security, notably protection against distributed denial-of-service attacks, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-180}}. Someone pays for all this. Content owners pay CDN operators to deliver their content, and the CDN in turn pays ISPs, carriers and network operators for hosting its servers in their data centers. The drawbacks are real too. A CDN can be expensive for high-traffic services. Some organizations and countries block popular CDN domains or IPs. And an audience far from any CDN server may see data travel farther.

sysd-blocks-181.title: Peer-to-peer: when every participant is also a server
sysd-blocks-181.text:
In a peer-to-peer network, nobody is only a customer. Peer-to-peer (P2P) is a distributed architecture in which participants share part of their own resources, such as processing power, storage or network capacity, directly with other peers. Each peer is both provider and requester, with no intermediary. The client-server model instead gives the roles to different participants.

Unstructured networks form by random connections, so they are easy to build and cope well with churn, peers frequently joining and leaving. Structured networks impose a topology so any node can efficiently find even a rare resource, most commonly with the design described in {{ref:sysd-scale-139}}. Decentralization removes the weak spot of client-server systems, a central server whose failure takes the whole service down, and capacity grows as nodes arrive. For content delivery, serving capacity can rise as more users fetch the content, which keeps the distributor's cost low. The catch is the freeloader problem. P2P systems reach full potential only when many nodes contribute, yet many users take without sharing, which can in some cases make the community collapse.

sysd-blocks-180.title: DDoS: a flood from many sources at once
sysd-blocks-180.text:
Sometimes the flood has no attacker: a link on a major site can deny service with the same effect as a DDoS attack. A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack makes a machine or network resource unavailable by flooding it with traffic that comes from many different sources. The sources are often thousands of malware-infected hosts in a botnet, so blocking a single source is not enough.

Common attacks are UDP flooding, SYN flooding and DNS amplification. A SYN flood leaves half-open connections that exhaust the server's available connections, because the forged sender address never replies. In a reflected attack, forged requests carrying the victim's spoofed address go to many computers, whose replies flood the victim. An application-layer (layer 7) attack over-exercises specific functions, such as search. It needs fewer resources and can look like legitimate traffic. Defense combines attack detection, traffic classification and response tools. Upstream filtering diverts traffic through a scrubbing center that passes only legitimate traffic, since DDoS can overwhelm any hardware firewall.

sysd-blocks-070.title: Origin and edge servers: where a CDN's content lives
sysd-blocks-070.text:
Where does a CDN's content really live? On the origin server, the primary source of content, which holds its original versions. The edge servers that cache and serve it are numerous and spread across the world. A CDN caches content in many geographic locations called edge locations, and each one holds several caching servers that deliver content to visitors in its proximity.

Providers serve a defined set of points of presence (PoPs), chosen for the coverage wanted, such as the United States, Asia-Pacific or global. PoPs are also called edges, edge nodes or edge networks. A CDN's footprint is the geographic area where its edge servers can effectively serve clients' requests. Size varies. Some CDNs have thousands of nodes and tens of thousands of servers on many remote PoPs. Others build a global network with only a small number of PoPs. An origin shield protects the origin during heavy traffic. DNS resolves the domain name to the IP address of the nearest edge server, and a control plane configures and manages the edge servers.

sysd-blocks-083.title: Image CDN: one picture, many versions
sysd-blocks-083.text: One image can need many versions. An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image over HTTP, depending on the properties of the requesting browser. The browser or server-side logic determines those properties. It generally combines three components: a CDN for fast serving of images, image manipulation and optimization, and device detection. Manipulation can happen on the fly through URL directives, in batch mode through manual upload of images, or fully automatically. Device detection reads the properties of the requesting browser or device from the User-Agent string, HTTP Accept headers, Client-Hints or JavaScript.

sysd-blocks-076.title: Peer-to-peer CDN: delivery that improves with demand
sysd-blocks-076.text: The more people want a file, the better a peer-to-peer CDN can perform. In a peer-to-peer CDN, clients provide resources as well as use them. CDN offloading is the mechanism that lets clients help deliver content to each other, in addition to edge server delivery. Unlike client-server systems, such a network can perform better as more users access the content, especially with protocols such as BitTorrent that require users to share. That keeps setup and running costs very small for the original content distributor. Web3 and blockchain technologies can also incentivize peers: nodes that take part receive crypto tokens in exchange for their involvement.

sysd-blocks-077.title: Private CDN: building your own delivery network
sysd-blocks-077.text: Content owners unsatisfied with the options or costs of a commercial CDN can build their own. A private CDN is made of PoPs that serve content only for that owner. Its PoPs can be caching servers, reverse proxies or application delivery controllers. It can be as simple as two caching servers or large enough to serve petabytes of content. Inside a company network it is also called an enterprise CDN, or eCDN. Large CDNs may likewise build their own private network to distribute copies of content across cache locations. They fall back on public networks when that network's capacity is insufficient or reduced by a failure.

sysd-blocks-079.title: Telco CDN: the network provider becomes the CDN
sysd-blocks-079.text: Streaming video grew so fast that telecommunications providers began launching CDNs of their own. A telco CDN runs on the network the provider owns, to lessen demands on the network backbone and reduce infrastructure investment. Telcos own the last mile, the final stretch of network to the customer. They can cache content deep in their networks, minimizing the distance video travels over the general Internet. They also have a built-in cost advantage, because traditional CDNs must lease bandwidth from telcos and build the operator's margin into their own costs. And running the delivery infrastructure gives operators control over resource utilization and better quality of service.

sysd-blocks-080.title: Virtual CDN: caches that appear where needed
sysd-blocks-080.text: A virtual CDN can create a cache wherever one is needed. A virtual CDN (vCDN), also called a software-defined CDN (sd-CDN), uses virtualization to deploy CDN caches dynamically. The aim is to reduce content provider costs while increasing elasticity and decreasing service delay. The virtual caches are deployed on physical servers across the provider's coverage. The two technologies they run on are covered in {{ref:sysd-reliab-065}} and {{ref:sysd-reliab-063}}. That avoids traditional CDN limits on performance, reliability and availability. Where a cache is placed depends on both the content type and the server or end-user location, so vCDNs significantly affect service delivery and network congestion.

sysd-blocks-071.title: CDN request flow: edge first, origin second
sysd-blocks-071.text:
The first request for a file at an edge location goes all the way to the origin. Later ones do not. Here is how a single request travels. After DNS resolution, the user's device sends its content request to the CDN edge server. The edge server checks its local cache for the content and, if it finds it, serves it to the user. If the content is not in the cache, the edge server forwards the request to the origin server. After receiving the content from the origin, the edge server stores a copy in its cache and delivers it to the user.

Once static assets are cached at a location, later requests there are served from its edge servers instead of the origin, which reduces origin load. Streaming follows a variation. The CDN receives the stream at its origin server and replicates it to many or all of its edge cache servers. Delivering it over HTTP then costs about the same as HTTP web caching.

sysd-blocks-072.title: Push and pull CDNs: who fills the cache
sysd-blocks-072.text:
CDNs differ in who fills the cache: the site owner or the first visitor. Push CDNs are sent new content whenever it changes. Pull CDNs fetch content from the origin when a user first requests it.

With a push CDN, the site owner uploads content directly to the CDN and rewrites URLs to point to it. The owner also configures when content expires and when it is updated. Content is uploaded only when it is new or changed, which minimizes traffic but maximizes storage, and it is placed once instead of re-pulled at regular intervals. That suits sites with little traffic or with content that is not often updated.

In a pull CDN the cache is updated on request. If the CDN lacks an asset, it fetches it from the origin, populates its cache and sends the asset to the user. Pull CDNs need less maintenance than push CDNs, because cache updates happen in response to client requests. They suit heavy-traffic sites, since traffic is spread more evenly and only recently requested content remains on the CDN. The same split holds for web caches in general: they are populated from user requests (pull caching) or from preloaded content disseminated by content servers (push caching).

sysd-blocks-073.title: CDN request routing: choosing which server answers
sysd-blocks-073.text: A CDN has many servers that could answer a request, so something must choose. Request routing directs each client request to the content source best able to serve it. That might be the service node closest to the client or the one with the most capacity. The algorithms include global server load balancing, DNS-based request routing, dynamic metafile generation, HTML rewriting and anycasting. Global server load balancing (GSLB) routes requests by factors such as geographic proximity, server load and network conditions. Anycast DNS lets multiple servers share the same IP address and helps route incoming traffic to the nearest data center. Proximity is estimated by probing, either reactive or proactive, and by watching live connections. Choosing for performance picks the fewest hops, the shortest time to the client or the highest server performance. Choosing for cost picks the cheapest locations. Edge servers near users tend to win on both. CDN providers also establish a presence at major Internet Exchange Points, so they can exchange traffic directly with ISPs and other networks.

sysd-blocks-074.title: Content networking techniques: intelligence at the edge
sysd-blocks-074.text: The Internet's core is deliberately simple. It follows the end-to-end principle: intelligence sits at the hosts and clients, so the core network only forwards data packets. A CDN adds intelligence as an overlay on top of that core, combining web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services. Web caches store popular content on servers close to the greatest demand, which reduces bandwidth requirements and server load and improves client response times. Server-load balancing shares traffic among servers or web caches, for example with a layer 4-7 switch holding one virtual IP address, adding capacity, reliability and health checks.

sysd-blocks-081.title: Edge content services: ICAP, OPES and Edge Side Includes
sysd-blocks-081.text: Some pages cannot simply be cached, because their content is generated. Changing catalogs and forums, or personalization, create a problem for caching systems. Content service protocols give access to content services, such as content adaptation and dynamic page assembly, distributed through a content network. ICAP, developed in the late 1990s, is an open standard for connecting application servers. The more recent OPES architecture lets service applications run on the OPES processor itself or remotely on a Callout Server. A group of companies also created Edge Side Includes (ESI), a small markup language for assembling dynamic web content at the edge.

sysd-blocks-075.title: End-user mapping: finding the client behind the resolver
sysd-blocks-075.text: A CDN may route a client in India to its edge server in Singapore, because that client uses a public DNS resolver in Singapore. CDNs traditionally located a client by the IP of its recursive DNS resolver. That performs poorly when the resolver is far away. End-user mapping fixes this. With the edns-client-subnet option, a CDN uses the IP address of the requesting client's subnet when resolving DNS requests. This drastically reduces round-trip latencies for clients on non-local resolvers. It has drawbacks. It reduces the effectiveness of caching resolutions at recursive resolvers, increases total DNS resolution traffic, and raises a privacy concern by exposing the client's subnet.

sysd-blocks-078.title: Multi-CDN: not trusting one network with a live event
sysd-blocks-078.text: High peak audiences, especially during live events, are why some content providers prefer not to rely on a single CDN. Multi-CDN means a provider combines several CDN services instead. Traffic can be split among them on the client side, on the server side at the origin, or on the cloud side between origin and audience. Selection criteria can be performance, availability and cost, and a CDN selector is the decision-making service that chooses among the CDNs. The IETF standardized a framework and request-routing interface for interconnecting CDNs, so a request can be redirected between them. Open Caching APIs let a provider use several CDNs consistently.

sysd-blocks-178.title: Edge computing: running the code near the user
sysd-blocks-178.text:
Running an application near its users, instead of in a centralized data center, can cut latency. Edge computing is a distributed computing model that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, and so to users. It is any design that pushes computation physically closer to a user. It generalizes the CDN idea. CDN nodes at the network edge prefetch and cache content and can customize it, and edge computing extends this by leveraging cloud infrastructure.

Processing locally avoids long transfers. Recognizing speech at the edge lets a system send text to the cloud instead of audio, cutting bandwidth. A voice assistant at the edge can keep serving local users during cloud or internet outages. The costs are real. Data traveling between nodes needs its own encryption, and edge nodes may be resource-constrained. Offloading every task to the edge can even slow things down because of transfer times between device and node, so the best configuration depends on the workload.

sysd-blocks-179.title: Subresource Integrity: checking what a CDN delivers
sysd-blocks-179.text: What if someone tampers with the scripts a CDN serves? Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C recommendation that protects website delivery. It validates assets served by a third party, such as a CDN, so they have not been compromised. The page author gives a cryptographic hash of the resource along with its location. The browser compares that hash with one computed from the fetched resource and discards the resource if they do not match. An integrity value may hold several expressions, each a hash algorithm name plus a Base64 digest, and the browser validates with the strongest recognized one. SRI works with JavaScript files and linked stylesheets.

sysd-blocks-082.title: CDN security and privacy: protection and its price
sysd-blocks-082.text: A CDN can shield a site, and it can also expose it. It can improve website security, especially against DDoS attacks. But CDNs serving JavaScript have been targeted to inject malicious content into pages. Subresource Integrity ensures a page loads only a script whose content matches a hash the site author references. Providers can profit from tracking data collected as their scripts load in the customer's browser origin. CDNs are therefore pointed out as potential privacy intrusions for behavioral targeting. A website using a CDN may violate the EU's GDPR: in 2021 a German court ruled that sending a visitor's IP address to a CDN violated it.

openers.content-delivery-networks: A content delivery network is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them. The origin server holds the original content, and the many edge servers spread around the world cache it and serve users nearby. A request is answered from the nearest edge server's cache, or the edge fetches the content from the origin, stores a copy and delivers it. This chapter follows that idea through the ways content reaches an edge, how requests find the right server and the variants built by content owners and telecommunications providers.

reviews.content-delivery-networks: A CDN moves content close to users by keeping copies on many edge servers while the origin server keeps the original. A request is answered from the edge's cache, or the edge fetches from the origin, and push and pull designs differ in who fills that cache. Request routing, from DNS to anycast and end-user mapping, picks which server answers, and a provider can combine several CDNs to avoid relying on one. Private, telco, virtual, image and peer-to-peer CDNs are variations on the same idea, built by different owners for different goals. Edge computing carries it from content to computation, and the same reach brings DDoS protection along with script-injection and privacy risks that Subresource Integrity helps to answer.
